intro: In the exam, every source comes with a caption and a question you have not seen before. The skill is the same each time: work out what the source is, who made it and why, what it suggests, and what it cannot tell you. Then write a short answer that names the source, adds your own dated knowledge, and goes beyond the obvious. Ten sources here. Four quick questions each, then a timed 3-mark answer.
checklist: Name the source and point to one detail in it
Add one fact of your own, with a date
Say what the detail suggests, not just what it shows
Go beyond the group or person named in the question

sources.caption: Scene from the Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidery made in England in the 1070s, probably ordered by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William the Conqueror's half-brother. The Latin caption reads 'Here King Harold is killed'.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary visual source made within about ten years of the event
A secondary source, because it was made after the battle
A primary written source
A secondary visual source made by a historian
qs.x: Made in the 1070s about 1066, by people on the winning side. A decade later is still 'at the time' for a medieval source. Written captions on it do not make it a written source.

qs.q: Who most likely wanted this made, and why?
o: The Normans, to present the conquest as rightful and Harold's death as deserved
The English, to mourn their king
The Church, to record a miracle
A later historian, to teach schoolchildren
qs.x: Odo was William's half-brother and fought at Hastings. The whole work tells the story from the Norman side, including Harold's broken oath. Purpose shapes what a source shows.

qs.q: What does the scene suggest about warfare in 1066?
o: Mounted knights in mail with kite shields and swords were the striking force
Battles were fought mainly with cannon
Soldiers fought without armour
Only kings took part in battle
qs.x: The horses, mail coats, long kite-shaped shields and swords are all visible details. 'Suggests' means you read the detail and draw a conclusion from it.

qs.q: What can this source NOT tell you reliably?
o: How the English saw the battle and its outcome
Whether Normans used horses
What a Norman knight's shield looked like
That Harold died at Hastings
qs.x: Everything shown is from the winners' point of view. For the English experience you would need a different source, such as the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain why the Battle of Hastings was a turning point for England.
sources.model: The source shows mounted Norman knights cutting down Harold's army and the caption confirms the king was killed, which suggests the English lost their leader and their chance to resist in one day. Hastings was a turning point because William then replaced almost the entire English ruling class with Normans, recorded every landholding in the Domesday Book of 1086, and imposed feudalism, so ordinary English people now answered to French-speaking lords and castles appeared across the country.
mark: Source detail named (knights, Harold's death) and what it suggests
Own knowledge with a date (Domesday 1086, Norman lords, castles)
Goes beyond the battle to the change for England and its people

sources.caption: Peasants reaping under the eye of a reeve, from the Queen Mary Psalter, an illuminated prayer book made in England around 1310 to 1320 for a wealthy owner.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary visual source: an illustration from a medieval manuscript
A photograph of a medieval harvest
A secondary source, because it is in a prayer book
A map of a manor
qs.x: An illumination is a painted picture in a manuscript. It was made in the period it shows, so it is primary and visual.

qs.q: Who made it and for whom, and why does that matter?
o: An artist for a rich patron; the peasants are shown by someone who did not share their life
Peasants, to record their own work
The king, to count his harvest
A monk, to teach farming
qs.x: Psalters were expensive prayer books for the wealthy. The scene is how the landowning class pictured the people who worked their land, which affects what it shows and leaves out.

qs.q: What does the detail of the reeve with a stick suggest?
o: Peasants' labour on the lord's land was supervised and could be enforced
Peasants worked whenever they chose
The reeve was also harvesting
Reaping was done by machines
qs.x: The reeve was the lord's manager. Standing over the workers with a stick suggests obligation and control, not free labour. That is an inference from a detail.

qs.q: Which question can this source NOT answer on its own?
o: How the peasants felt about this work
That reaping was done by hand with sickles
That women as well as men worked in the fields
That a supervisor was present
qs.x: The picture shows bodies, tools and a supervisor. Feelings are not visible; to say peasants resented it you would need a written source or your own knowledge of the 1381 revolt.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain what the source suggests about the lives of peasants on a medieval manor.
sources.model: The source shows men and women cutting grain with sickles while a reeve stands over them with a stick, which suggests their labour on the lord's land was compulsory and watched. This fits what we know of the manor: serfs owed days of work on the lord's demesne, paid rents in produce and needed permission to marry or leave, so their lives were controlled by the lord's needs. It was only after the Black Death of 1347 cut the workforce that peasants could begin to demand wages instead.
mark: Detail named (reeve, sickles) and what it suggests (supervised, compulsory)
Own knowledge: demesne labour, permissions, a date
Goes beyond the picture to how the system worked and when it changed

sources.text: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any other way, nor will we proceed with force against him, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.
sources.caption: Adapted from clause 39 of Magna Carta, the charter King John was forced to agree to by his barons at Runnymede in June 1215.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary written source: a legal document from the time
A secondary source written by a historian
A primary visual source
A letter from the king
qs.x: A charter is a formal legal document. It was written in 1215 about the rules of 1215, so it is primary and written.

qs.q: Who forced this to be written, and why?
o: The barons, to stop John ruling by force and taxing without consent
John, to increase his power
The Pope, to punish John
The peasants, to end serfdom
qs.x: John had lost Normandy, raised heavy taxes and punished barons without trial. The barons rebelled and made him seal the charter. The purpose tells you whose interests it protects.

qs.q: What does the clause suggest about the king's power?
o: The king was now expected to act under the law rather than above it
The king could do whatever he wished
The barons had replaced the king
The law did not apply to anyone
qs.x: 'Lawful judgement' and 'law of the land' put a limit on the king's actions. That is a change from the idea that the king's will was law.

qs.q: Which detail shows the limit of this clause?
o: 'Free man' excluded serfs, who were most of the population
It mentions imprisonment
It mentions the law of the land
It was written in June
qs.x: Most English people in 1215 were unfree. The charter protected barons and freemen, not the peasants on the manor. Noticing who is left out is a mark-earning skill.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain how Magna Carta shows a change in the power of the king.
sources.model: The clause says no free man can be imprisoned or lose his property 'except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land', which suggests the king could no longer act purely on his own will. This was a change because John had taxed heavily and punished barons without trial after losing Normandy in 1204, and in 1215 the barons forced him to seal the charter at Runnymede. However, the protection was for 'free men', so for serfs, the majority, the king's power and their lord's power stayed much the same.
mark: Quotes a phrase and says what it suggests
Own knowledge with a date (Normandy 1204, Runnymede 1215, the barons' revolt)
Goes beyond the barons to note who the clause did not protect

sources.text: The deaths began in Siena in May. It was a cruel and terrible thing. Fathers abandoned their children, wives their husbands and brothers each other, because people believed the sickness passed through breath and sight. Nobody could be found to bury the dead, for money or for friendship. I buried five of my own children with my own hands.
sources.caption: Adapted from the chronicle of Agnolo di Tura, a shoemaker and tax collector in Siena, Italy, writing about the plague of 1348.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary written source: an eyewitness chronicle
A secondary source written long after
A government record of deaths
A medical textbook
qs.x: A chronicle written by a man who lived through the event is primary and written. His job as a tax collector also means he was used to recording things.

qs.q: Why is the writer's own loss important for how you use the source?
o: It makes him a reliable witness to the suffering but may colour his view of other people's behaviour
It means the source is useless
It shows he was a doctor
It proves the plague started in Siena
qs.x: Grief gives the account power and truth about what the plague felt like. It may also make his claims about everyone abandoning everyone sound more total than they were. Say both.

qs.q: What does 'nobody could be found to bury the dead' suggest?
o: Normal community and religious customs collapsed under the scale of death
Siena had no cemeteries
People did not care about their relatives
Burial was illegal
qs.x: In a Catholic society, proper burial mattered enormously. That it could not be bought or asked of friends suggests the number of deaths overwhelmed the normal order.

qs.q: What can this source NOT tell you?
o: How many people died across Europe
That the writer lost children
That people believed the disease spread through breath
That the plague reached Siena in 1348
qs.x: One man in one city cannot give the European figure. For the estimate of around a third of the population you need historians' work, which is your own knowledge.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain the impact of the Black Death on medieval communities.
sources.model: Agnolo di Tura writes that families abandoned each other and 'nobody could be found to bury the dead', which suggests that fear of the sickness broke down the normal bonds of family and religion. His account of burying five of his own children shows the scale of death in a single household. Across Europe the plague of 1347 to 1351 killed around a third of the population, and the shortage of workers that followed let surviving labourers demand higher wages, which in England led to the Statute of Labourers in 1351 and helped cause the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
mark: Quotes the source and infers (bonds broke down, scale of death)
Own knowledge with dates (a third of Europe, 1351, 1381)
Goes beyond Siena to the wider social and economic change

sources.caption: The samurai Takezaki Suenaga charging Mongol soldiers, from the Mongol Invasion Scrolls, Japan, around 1293. Suenaga had the scrolls made himself.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary visual source: a painted scroll made soon after the invasions
A secondary source, because it is a painting
A primary written source
A photograph
qs.x: Painted about twelve years after the 1281 invasion, by order of a man who fought in it. Primary and visual.

qs.q: Why did Suenaga have the scrolls made?
o: To record his own deeds so he could claim a reward from the shogunate
To warn Japan about the Mongols
To teach children about history
To honour the Mongol soldiers
qs.x: Suenaga travelled to Kamakura to argue he deserved land for his bravery. The scrolls are his evidence. This is why he is always at the centre of the action.

qs.q: What does the scene suggest about how the two sides fought?
o: Samurai charged on horseback as individuals, while the Mongols fought in groups with bows and exploding bombs
Both sides used the same tactics
The Mongols had no weapons
The samurai fought on foot
qs.x: The horse, the single charging samurai, the grouped archers and the bursting bomb are all details in the picture. Reading them together gives you an inference about tactics.

qs.q: What should make you careful about using this source?
o: Suenaga paid for it to make himself look brave, so his role may be exaggerated
It was painted in Japan
It shows horses
It is very old
qs.x: Purpose shapes content. A source made to win a reward will put its owner in the best light. It is still useful for weapons, armour and tactics.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain why the Mongol invasions weakened the Kamakura shogunate.
sources.model: The scroll shows Suenaga charging alone into Mongol archers, and he had it painted to prove he deserved a reward, which suggests samurai expected land in return for fighting. The invasions of 1274 and 1281 were defeated, with the help of the typhoon the Japanese called the kamikaze, but no enemy land was captured, so the shogunate had nothing to give the thousands of samurai who had fought. Suenaga himself had to travel to Kamakura to get his claim heard. Unpaid and resentful warriors stopped trusting the shogunate, which helped its collapse in 1333.
mark: Detail and purpose of the source used to infer (land for service)
Own knowledge with dates (1274, 1281, kamikaze, 1333)
Goes beyond the battle to the system of reward and its failure

sources.text: The samurai must devote themselves to study and to the military arts. Even repairs to a castle must be reported to the shogunate; new building is strictly forbidden. Marriages between daimyo families must not be arranged privately. Daimyo must not shelter men who have plotted rebellion or committed crimes in another domain.
sources.caption: Adapted from the Buke Shohatto (Laws for the Military Houses), issued by the Tokugawa shogunate in 1615, shortly after the fall of Osaka Castle.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary written source: a law code issued by the government of the time
A secondary source describing the laws
A letter from a daimyo
A primary visual source
qs.x: A set of laws issued in 1615 by the shogunate is an official primary written source.

qs.q: Why did the shogunate issue these laws in 1615?
o: Having just destroyed the last Toyotomi stronghold, Ieyasu wanted to stop daimyo from ever building the strength to challenge the Tokugawa
To make samurai better soldiers for a coming war
To encourage castle building
To promote marriage
qs.x: Osaka Castle fell in 1615, ending the last serious rival. The timing shows purpose: lock in Tokugawa control while the daimyo were weak.

qs.q: What does the rule on marriages suggest?
o: Marriage was a way daimyo built alliances, and the shogunate wanted to control that
The shogunate disapproved of marriage
Daimyo were not allowed to marry
Marriage was unimportant to samurai
qs.x: Alliances through marriage had fuelled the civil wars of the 1400s and 1500s. Controlling marriages controlled alliances. That is an inference from a rule.

qs.q: What does this source NOT tell you?
o: Whether the daimyo obeyed, or how they felt about the laws
That castle building was restricted
That samurai were expected to study
That the laws came from the shogunate
qs.x: A law tells you what the government wanted. Whether it worked needs other evidence, such as the 250 years of peace that followed, which is your own knowledge.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain how the Tokugawa shogunate used laws like this to control the daimyo.
sources.model: The law bans new castles and private marriages between daimyo families, which suggests the shogunate feared the alliances and fortresses that had allowed daimyo to fight each other during the Onin War and after. Issued in 1615, just after Osaka Castle fell, it was followed in 1635 by compulsory sankin kotai, which forced daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo and leave their families there as hostages, draining their money on processions. Together these rules meant that for over two centuries no daimyo had the castles, allies or funds to rebel, which is why Japan stayed at peace until Perry's arrival in 1853.
mark: Names a rule from the source and infers its purpose
Own knowledge with dates (1615 Osaka, 1635 sankin kotai)
Goes beyond the law to its effect on daimyo and on Japan

sources.caption: A Dutch ship arriving at Dejima, painted by Kawahara Keiga, a Japanese artist in Nagasaki who worked for the Dutch traders, around 1811.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary visual source: a painting made in the period by someone who saw the scene
A secondary source, because the artist was Japanese
A photograph of Nagasaki
A map of Japan
qs.x: Keiga lived in Nagasaki and painted what the Dutch asked him to record. A painting from the time, of the time, is primary and visual.

qs.q: Why does it matter that the artist worked for the Dutch?
o: He had rare access to Dejima and foreign ships, but his paintings were made to please Dutch buyers
It makes the source secondary
It means he was not Japanese
It means the painting is in Dutch
qs.x: Few Japanese could see Dejima up close. That makes Keiga valuable. But a painter working for clients shows what the clients want, so purpose still matters.

qs.q: What does the arrival of a single foreign ship, watched by onlookers, suggest about sakoku?
o: Foreign contact was rare and tightly controlled, so a ship's arrival was an event
Japan traded freely with all nations
The Dutch controlled Nagasaki
Nobody in Japan was interested in foreigners
qs.x: Under sakoku only the Dutch and Chinese could trade, and only at Nagasaki. One ship a year or so was worth painting. The crowd suggests curiosity, not hostility.

qs.q: What can the source NOT show you?
o: What the shogunate thought about foreign ideas, or how goods were used across Japan
That ships came to Nagasaki
That Japanese people watched the arrival
That the Dutch had a trading post
qs.x: A harbour scene shows a moment in one place. The policy behind it and the spread of Dutch learning (rangaku) across Japan come from your own knowledge.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain the significance of Dejima for Japan under sakoku.
sources.model: The painting shows a single Dutch ship arriving while Japanese onlookers watch, which suggests that foreign contact was rare enough to be an event and that the shogunate kept it confined to one place. Dejima was significant because after the sakoku edicts of the 1630s it was the only point where Western goods and knowledge could enter Japan: Dutch books on medicine and science, called rangaku, reached Japanese scholars through it. So while sakoku kept Christianity and foreign armies out for over 200 years, Dejima meant Japan was never completely closed, which helped it respond quickly to the West after 1853.
mark: Detail named (one ship, onlookers) and what it suggests
Own knowledge with dates (1630s edicts, rangaku, 1853)
Goes beyond the harbour to Japan as a whole

sources.caption: Official photograph of Emperor Meiji by Uchida Kuichi, 1873. Copies were sent to government offices and schools across Japan.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary visual source: an official photograph from the time
A painting of the emperor
A secondary source, because it is a copy
A primary written source
qs.x: A photograph taken in 1873 of the ruler of 1873 is a primary visual source, even if you see a reproduction of it.

qs.q: Why did the government distribute this image?
o: To present a modern, Western-style emperor as the symbol of the new Japan
To sell copies to tourists
To show the emperor's private life
Because photography was cheap
qs.x: Until 1868 the emperor had been hidden in Kyoto. Sending a photograph of him in a military uniform to every school was a way of making him the face of modernisation.

qs.q: What do the uniform, short hair and chair suggest?
o: The Meiji government wanted Japan to look like a modern Western power
The emperor had joined a foreign army
Japan had been conquered
Traditional dress was banned for everyone
qs.x: Each detail is a deliberate choice: the Western uniform, the European-style haircut, the posed seat. Read them together and the message is 'modern and equal to the West'.

qs.q: What does the source NOT tell you?
o: How ordinary Japanese people felt about the changes
That the emperor wore a Western uniform
That the photograph was taken in 1873
That the government used images of the emperor
qs.x: A staged official portrait shows the government's message, not the public's reaction. For how samurai or peasants felt you need other sources or your own knowledge of the 1877 rebellion and tax protests.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain what the photograph suggests about the aims of the Meiji government.
sources.model: The emperor is shown in a Western military uniform with short hair, seated on a European chair, which suggests the government wanted Japan to be seen as a modern nation equal to the Western powers. After the Restoration of 1868 the government did exactly that: it introduced conscription in 1873, the same year as this photograph, built railways and telegraphs, and sent the Iwakura Mission abroad to study Western systems. The image was sent to schools because the government also wanted ordinary people to feel loyalty to the emperor rather than to their old daimyo, which shows the aim was to unite the country as well as modernise it.
mark: Details named (uniform, hair, chair) and what they suggest
Own knowledge with dates (1868, 1873 conscription, Iwakura Mission)
Goes beyond the emperor to what the government wanted from ordinary people

sources.text: 1. Assemblies shall be set up and all matters decided by open discussion. 2. All classes, high and low, shall unite in carrying out the affairs of the state. 3. The common people, no less than officials and warriors, shall be allowed to follow their own callings so that there is no discontent. 4. Bad customs of the past shall be broken off. 5. Knowledge shall be sought throughout the world to strengthen the rule of the emperor.
sources.caption: Adapted from the Charter Oath, sworn by the Meiji Emperor in April 1868 at the start of his reign.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary written source: an official statement of government aims
A secondary source summarising Meiji policy
A private letter
A primary visual source
qs.x: An oath sworn by the emperor in 1868 is an official primary document. It states intentions, which is different from recording what happened.

qs.q: Why was the oath issued at this moment?
o: The new government had just taken power from the shogun and needed to win support and set a direction
To declare war on the West
To restore the Tokugawa
To end the Meiji period
qs.x: The shogun had resigned in late 1867 and fighting continued into 1868. An oath promising discussion, unity and knowledge was a way of reassuring the daimyo, samurai and commoners.

qs.q: What does article 3 suggest about the Tokugawa period?
o: The old class system had fixed people's occupations by birth and caused resentment
Commoners had always been free to choose work
Warriors were to lose all their rights immediately
Officials were to become farmers
qs.x: Saying commoners 'shall be allowed' to follow their own callings implies they were not before. The four-class system had fixed status by birth for over 250 years.

qs.q: What does the oath NOT tell you?
o: Whether the promises were kept, or how quickly
That the emperor wanted knowledge from abroad
That assemblies were promised
That the oath came in 1868
qs.x: Aims are not outcomes. The first elected assembly, the Diet, did not meet until 1890. Checking a promise against what happened is where your own knowledge earns marks.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain how the Charter Oath marked a break from the Tokugawa period.
sources.model: The oath promises that 'all classes, high and low' will share in government and that 'knowledge shall be sought throughout the world', which suggests a deliberate rejection of both the fixed four-class system and the sakoku policy of the Tokugawa. These promises were acted on: the domains were abolished in 1871, commoners were conscripted from 1873 and the Iwakura Mission toured America and Europe from 1871 to 1873. However, article 1's promise of assemblies was slow to arrive, since the Diet did not meet until 1890, so the break was sharper for samurai, who lost their status, than for commoners, who gained a vote only much later.
mark: Quotes the oath and infers what it rejects
Own knowledge with dates (1871, 1873, 1890)
Goes beyond the promise to who gained and lost, and how fast

sources.caption: Studio photograph of a samurai in full armour, Japan, 1860s, photographer unknown. Photographs like this were sold to foreign visitors in Yokohama.

qs.q: What type of source is this?
o: A primary visual source: a photograph taken in the period
A painting of a samurai
A secondary source, because the photographer is unknown
A primary written source
qs.x: Taken in the 1860s of a man of the 1860s. Not knowing the photographer's name does not make it secondary; it just means you say 'photographer unknown' when you name the origin.

qs.q: Why was it made, and why does that matter?
o: To sell to foreigners who wanted an 'exotic' samurai, so the pose and armour are staged
To record a battle
As an official government portrait
To train soldiers
qs.x: By the 1860s full armour was ceremonial; samurai did not walk about dressed like this. A souvenir photograph shows what the buyer expected, which is a purpose to name.

qs.q: What does the photograph suggest about samurai identity in the 1860s?
o: Armour and swords still mattered as symbols of status even though samurai rarely fought
Samurai were constantly at war
Samurai had already given up their swords
Samurai wore Western dress
qs.x: Two centuries of peace had made samurai officials, but the armour and two swords remained the marks of their class. The photo preserves the symbol, not the daily reality.

qs.q: What can it NOT show you?
o: What happened to samurai after 1868, or how this man lived day to day
That samurai carried swords
That armour was still owned in the 1860s
That photography existed in Japan by the 1860s
qs.x: A single staged moment cannot show the decade that followed: conscription in 1873, the sword ban in 1876 and the loss of stipends. That is your own knowledge to add.

sources.write: Using the source and your own knowledge, explain how the position of the samurai changed in the years after this photograph was taken.
sources.model: The photograph shows a samurai in full armour with his swords, which suggests that in the 1860s these were still the proud symbols of a warrior class, even though after 250 years of Tokugawa peace most samurai worked as officials. Within fifteen years that status was gone: the Meiji government introduced conscription in 1873 so commoners filled the army, banned the wearing of swords in 1876 and replaced samurai rice stipends with bonds. Some samurai rebelled in 1877 and were defeated by the conscript army, which shows the change was permanent, while others became officers, officials and businessmen in the new Japan.
mark: Details named (armour, swords) and what they suggest
Own knowledge with dates (1873, 1876, 1877)
Goes beyond this one man to the whole class and what became of them
